title: Breakup of Pangaea
summary: From about 201 million years ago the supercontinent Pangaea came apart: the Central Atlantic opened amid the CAMP flood basalts, Laurasia and Gondwana separated, the South Atlantic unzipped, and India drifted north into Asia.
card: Pangaea, welded together when Gondwana and Laurussia collided in the late Paleozoic, began rifting in the Triassic and split apart from about 201 million years ago. The first break ran between North America and northwest Africa, where the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupted at the same moment as the end-Triassic mass extinction. Over the next 150 million years the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans opened and India crossed the Tethys to meet Asia.
what:
Pangaea was the supercontinent that gathered almost all of Earth's continental crust in the late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic. It assembled as the Rheic Ocean closed: Gondwana and Laurussia were largely joined by the Mississippian, and West Africa and South America sutured onto North America during the Carboniferous and early Permian, raising the Variscan, Alleghanian and Ouachita mountain belts in collisions spanning roughly 380 to 290 million years ago (Ma). The last additions, the North and South China blocks, docked in the Triassic.

Breakup had a long run-up. Rifts began opening inside Pangaea around 240 Ma, and by the end of the Triassic rift basins such as the Fundy, Newark and Argana basins lined the future margins of eastern North America and Morocco. About 201.5 Ma the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) erupted and intruded across this rift zone and far beyond it, from the Amazon basin to Iberia; a 1999 study estimated its extent at about 7 million km² and its magma volume at about 2 million km³. High-precision zircon dates place the first CAMP pulses at the same time as the end-Triassic mass extinction, about 201.56 Ma, although whether the eruptions caused the extinction is still argued.

Seafloor spreading then separated North America from northwest Africa, cutting the northern landmass, Laurasia, from the southern one, Gondwana. When spreading began is disputed: older models put the oldest Central Atlantic ocean crust in the Middle Jurassic, while reinterpretations of magnetic anomalies and salt basins push it back to about 195–190 Ma. Gondwana split into eastern and western halves in the Early Jurassic. Between about 140 and 103 Ma South America and Africa pulled apart from south to north, opening the South Atlantic. Greater India left Australia–Antarctica around 136–126 Ma and Madagascar around 94–84 Ma, then moved rapidly north and collided with Asia about 50–40 Ma.

Alfred Wegener argued from 1912 that the continents had once been joined and later named the supercontinent Pangaea; confirming evidence arrived only from the mid-1950s.

uncertainty.note: Start is set at the CAMP eruptions and end-Triassic extinction (c. 201.5 Ma), the conventional moment of breakup; intracontinental rifting began c. 240 Ma (Müller et al. 2019). Onset of Central Atlantic seafloor spreading is disputed (c. 195–190 Ma vs Middle Jurassic). End is set at India's collision with Asia, dated 50–40 Ma; plate motion continues today.

how: Breakup was driven by extension of the continental lithosphere. From about 240 Ma Pangaea stretched along networks of rifts; by the latest Triassic, fault-bounded basins such as Fundy, Newark and Argana had filled with river, lake and dune sediments. Around 201.5 Ma huge volumes of basaltic magma rose into and through these basins and far beyond them as dykes, sills and lava flows: the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province. Its main eruptive phase lasted a few hundred thousand years, and gases released from the magma and from heated carbon-rich basin sediments are the leading explanation for the end-Triassic extinction. Continental crust then gave way to new ocean crust formed at a mid-ocean ridge. In one model, Central Atlantic spreading ran very slowly (about 0.8 cm a year) for its first 20 million years, sped up to about 1.7 cm a year after a change of direction at about 170 Ma, and produced more crust on the American side. Breakup was diachronous elsewhere: the South Atlantic rift extended slowly east–west from 140 Ma, localised strain from about 126 Ma, and broke up from south to north between about 113 and 103 Ma. In the east, a ridge between Greater India and Australia–Antarctica propagated from about 136 Ma, and after a reorganisation near 100 Ma India separated from Madagascar. India's northward motion, about 9 cm a year near 80 Ma, closed the Tethys and ended in collision with Asia. Wegener could not name a force able to move continents, the main objection raised against him; plate tectonics later supplied one.
why_it_matters: The breakup of Pangaea made the map of the modern world. It opened the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, set the Americas apart from Africa and Europe, isolated Antarctica, Australia and India, and by the end of the Cretaceous had brought most continents close to their present shapes. Its opening act, the CAMP eruptions, coincides with the end-Triassic mass extinction, which removed roughly half of marine species and cleared the way for dinosaurs to dominate land for the rest of the Mesozoic. Its closing act, India's collision with Asia, began raising the Himalaya, which still rise by more than 1 cm a year. The rifts left behind built the passive margins on both sides of the South Atlantic, including the pre-salt basins of Brazil and Angola. Without the breakup there would be no Atlantic Ocean between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia, no Himalaya, and the separate evolutionary histories of island continents such as Australia would not have unfolded the same way. The breakup also mattered for science: matching coastlines, fossils and rocks on opposite sides of the Atlantic led Wegener to propose continental drift in 1912, an idea rejected for decades that became a foundation of plate tectonics once seafloor evidence arrived from the mid-1950s. Today the record drives the Atlas's ambient Plates layer between about 240 and 50 Ma.

perspectives.holder: Earlier kinematic models of the Central Atlantic (as characterised by Sahabi et al. 2004 and Labails et al. 2010)
perspectives.account: The oldest ocean crust between North America and northwest Africa is of Middle Jurassic age, so seafloor spreading began well after the CAMP eruptions.

perspectives.holder: Sahabi, Aslanian and Olivet (2004); Labails, Olivet, Aslanian and Roest (2010)
perspectives.account: A reinterpretation of the West African magnetic anomaly and the Moroccan and Nova Scotian salt basins places the first ocean crust in the Late Sinemurian, about 195–190 Ma, roughly 20 million years earlier, followed by very slow spreading.

perspectives.holder: Schoene et al. (2010); Whiteside et al. (2010); Blackburn et al. (2013, as cited by Oliveira et al. 2023)
perspectives.account: CAMP volcanism began within the resolution of high-precision dating of the end-Triassic extinction and is the strongest case for a volcanic cause of a mass extinction.

The causal link between CAMP and the extinction remains debated; recalculated ages show the dated North Mountain Basalt post-dates the continental extinction by almost 80,000 years, pointing to earlier intrusions such as the Brazilian sills.

importance.justification: The breakup of Pangaea created today's oceans and continents, is tied to one of the five great mass extinctions, and is the backbone of the Atlas's deep-time Plates layer.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the onset age of Central Atlantic seafloor spreading (Middle Jurassic vs c. 195–190 Ma), of CAMP's total area (only the 1999 figure was verified), and of the pin's paleo-latitude, which spans about 17 degrees between plate models.
